title: Lean tools in Microsoft 365: a playbook for SQDC, Gemba, A3 and 5S
summary: Maps each Lean routine (tier meetings, SQDC, Gemba walk, A3, kaizen, 5S) to a concrete Microsoft 365 home with columns, owners, cadence and a worked example, so digital tools support the Gemba instead of replacing it.
body:
# Lean tools in Microsoft 365: a playbook for SQDC, Gemba, A3 and 5S

## Purpose
Lean routines work because they are short, visual and happen at the place of work. Microsoft 365 does not replace that. It gives the routines a memory (actions do not get lost), a shared view across shifts and sites, and numbers you do not have to collect by hand. This playbook says where each routine lives, which columns you need, who owns it and how often it runs.

## Prerequisites
- Microsoft 365 with Teams, SharePoint, Lists and Planner. Power Apps and Power Automate are optional; check which of them your frontline licenses include (Microsoft's frontline overview notes that F3 includes some features F1 does not, such as Power Apps and Power Automate).
- One owner per routine (not one for "digital Lean").
- A physical board or wall stays where it already works. Digital is the record and the roll-up.

## The mapping
| Routine | Cadence | Where it lives | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 shift start (SQDC) | 10 min, every shift | Board at the line, numbers from a Power BI page | Team leader | Actions into the action register |
| Tier 2 line review | 15 min daily | Teams channel for the area plus the same Power BI page | Area manager | Escalations, resource decisions |
| Tier 3 plant review | 30 min weekly | Teams meeting with the list views | Plant manager | Decisions, funding, cross-area topics |
| Gemba walk | Weekly per leader | Microsoft Forms or a Power Apps form writing to a list | Each leader | Observations, linked actions |
| A3 problem solving | Per problem | One list item plus an attached A3 file | A3 owner and coach | Countermeasures, results |
| Kaizen ideas | Continuous | List with a simple form | CI coordinator | Ideas, pilots, savings |
| 5S audit | Monthly per zone | Form or Power Apps checklist into a list | Zone owner | Score, photos, actions |

## Build: one action register for everything
Create a Microsoft Lists list "Actions" on the plant site. Every routine writes here, so nobody searches five places.
Columns: Title (text), Source (choice: Tier1, Tier2, Tier3, Gemba, A3, Kaizen, 5S, Audit), Area (choice), Owner (person), Due date (date), Status (choice: Open, In progress, Done, Cancelled), Priority (choice: A, B, C), Linked item (hyperlink), Closed on (date), Effect verified (yes/no).
Views: My open actions (filter Owner is me, Status not Done), Overdue (Due date before today, status open), Per area (grouped).
Rule: an action without owner and due date is not an action. Make Owner and Due date required columns.

## Build: Gemba observations
List "Gemba observations": Date, Area, Observer (person), Process step (choice or text), Observation type (choice: Waste, Safety, Quality, Standard not followed, Good practice), What I saw (multi-line), Waste category (choice with the eight wastes), Action created (yes/no).
The form opens from a QR code on the tablet or phone. Keep it to five fields; long forms get skipped.

## Build: A3 and kaizen
- A3: the one-page thinking matters more than the tool. Use a list item per A3 (Title, Owner, Coach, Start, Target date, Status, Root cause category, Result) with the A3 document attached from a Word or PowerPoint template. Review progress in the weekly Tier 3 view.
- Kaizen: columns Idea, Submitter, Area, Expected effect, Status (New, Reviewed, Pilot, Implemented, Rejected with reason), Decision date. Promise an answer within a fixed number of days, and keep the promise.

## Teams conventions
Create one channel per area for Tier 2 and pin the Power BI page and the "Per area" Actions view as tabs. Note: shared channels support tabs except Stream, Planner and Forms (per Microsoft Learn on shared channels), so do not plan Planner or Forms tabs in a shared channel.

## RACI
| Activity | Team leader | Area manager | CI coordinator | IT/Power Platform admin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Run Tier 1 | R/A | I | I | - |
| Maintain action register | R | A | C | C |
| Gemba form design | C | C | R/A | C |
| Monthly 5S score roll-up | R | A | R | I |
| Access and lifecycle of lists | I | C | C | R/A |

## Worked example (invented data)
Line 3, early shift. The Power BI page shows quality 98.1 percent first pass yield against a target of 98.5 and delivery red because of a missing carton. The team leader raises two actions in the register: "Check carton supplier delivery slot" (owner: logistics lead, due: tomorrow 12:00) and "Review glue temperature setting after 3 rejects" (owner: process technician, due: today 14:00). At Tier 2 the area manager sees both in the "Per area" view, and the carton action is escalated because the owner needs a purchasing decision. At Friday's Gemba walk the plant manager notes "Stop sign used as a shelf" and creates a 5S action. Count at week end: 14 actions opened, 11 closed, 3 open, 1 of them overdue (closure rate 11 / 14 = 79 percent); the overdue item is discussed first on Monday.

## Common mistakes
- Five tools for five routines. Use one register.
- Dashboards nobody discusses. A KPI without a meeting is decoration.
- Naming operators in observations. Record the process, not the person; involve the works council or data protection officer before any person-related data collection.
- Digitising a bad routine. Fix the 10-minute meeting first.
- Starting with Power Apps. Start with Lists and Forms and move to Power Apps when a real need shows up.

## Adapt to your environment
Replace the choice lists with your own area names and waste categories, set cadences to your shift model, and check licensing and data residency with your IT team. Review who can see observations: a plant-wide list may need item-level permissions for sensitive topics.

title: AS9100 evidence map in SharePoint: document control, records and audit-ready libraries
summary: A practical way to organise audit evidence in SharePoint: libraries, metadata, approval and version settings, record labels and an evidence card per process, without quoting clause numbers you must check in the standard.
body:
# AS9100 evidence map in SharePoint: document control, records and audit-ready libraries

## Purpose
Auditors do not ask for your folder structure; they ask for proof. AS9100 builds on ISO 9001 and adds topics such as risk, product safety, configuration management, supplier quality, traceability, operational control, documented information, corrective and preventive action and internal audits. This entry shows how to organise evidence in SharePoint so each question has a known place, an owner and a short path. It does not quote clause numbers. Check the current standard text, your certification body's expectations and your own quality manual.

## Prerequisites
- SharePoint Online with content approval and versioning available on libraries; Microsoft Purview retention labels if you want records protection.
- A QMS owner who decides document status rules.
- A decision on which system is the system of record for each item (SharePoint, ERP, MES or the MRO system). Do not duplicate records.

## The evidence card
Make one card per process area (one page, stored with the process). It prevents "where did we put that?" in the audit room.
Fields: Process area, Process owner, Evidence question the auditor is likely to ask, Where the evidence is (link), Format (document, record, list item, system report), Retention class, Last checked on, Checked by.

## Evidence map (starting set)
| Topic area | Typical question | Evidence | Home | Key metadata |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Documented information | Is the current revision in use, and who approved it? | Procedure with approval and version history | Library "QMS Effective" | Doc number, Revision, Status, Effective date, Next review |
| Document change | What changed and why? | Change request with review result | List "Document changes" | Doc number, Reason, Approver, Date |
| Training and acknowledgement | Did the staff read the new revision? | Read-and-sign result | Forms or list | Doc number, Revision, Person, Date |
| Supplier quality | Is the supplier approved and are certificates valid? | Approval record, certificates | List "Approved suppliers" plus library | Supplier, Scope, Certificate expiry, Next audit |
| Operational control | Was the work done under the current instruction? | Work instruction, inspection record | MES or library | Part number, Order number |
| Nonconformity and CAPA | Was the cause removed and was it effective? | NCR and CAPA records | List "NCR-CAPA" | Cause, Owner, Due, Evidence, Verified on, Effectiveness check |
| Internal audits | Is the programme risk-based and complete? | Audit plan, reports, findings | List "Audit plan" plus library | Process, Auditor, Date, Findings |
| Configuration and traceability | Can you trace a part to its documents? | Records linked by number | MES or ERP | Part, Serial or batch |

## Library settings that matter
- Separate "Effective" from "Draft" and "Archive". Only effective documents are visible to all staff. Superseded revisions move to an archive with restricted read access. This also keeps search and Copilot from citing old revisions.
- Turn on content approval, and major and minor versions, so a draft is not visible to readers before approval. Check how it behaves in your tenant, because the planning article on versioning is written for SharePoint Server and Microsoft 365 behaviour should be confirmed.
- Version limits: Microsoft documents automatic and manual limits; the UI does not allow fewer than 100 major versions or an expiry under 30 days for manual limits. Items under a retention policy or hold ignore library version limits, and versions of records cannot be deleted. Choose automatic trimming only if you are sure the approval trail lives elsewhere (for example the change list).
- Record labels: Microsoft Purview distinguishes a standard label, a record (locked or unlocked) and a regulatory record. A locked record blocks editing and deleting content (an unlocked record can still be edited, but not deleted); a regulatory record cannot be unlabeled by anybody, not even a global administrator, cannot be auto-applied and must be enabled with PowerShell. Use a locked record label for released inspection results; use regulatory records only when a legal or regulatory reason exists and your legal team agrees.

## Worked example (invented data)
Work instruction WI-0142, revision C, is released. The document owner changes metadata Status from "In review" to "Effective", sets Effective date and Next review, and the approver approves in the library. A flow moves revision B to the archive, a second flow creates read-and-sign tasks for the 23 operators in group "Line 3 Operators". Two weeks later an auditor asks for proof. The evidence card for "Documented information" leads to: the library version history (who approved and when), the change list entry (why), and the read-and-sign list (22 of 23 done, one on leave with a due date). The gap is explained rather than discovered.

## RACI
| Task | QMS owner | Process owner | IT admin | Auditor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Define metadata and status rules | A/R | C | C | I |
| Approve and release documents | A | R | - | I |
| Library settings and labels | A | I | R | I |
| Quarterly evidence-card check | A | R | - | C |

## Common mistakes
- Using folders for status. Use metadata and views.
- One giant library with no indexed columns. Index Doc number, Status and Process area early; SharePoint has a 5,000-item list view threshold that cannot be changed in SharePoint Online, and a limit of 30 million items per library.
- Declaring everything a record. Locked content blocks normal corrections.
- Expecting SharePoint to be a full QMS tool. It is a good document and record base; workflows around it need design.

## Adapt to your environment
Use your own document numbering, status names and retention classes from the quality manual. Keep aviation-specific retention periods out of this build until your quality manager has confirmed them against the current regulation and your own manuals.

title: Copilot readiness check for a manufacturing plant: manuals, shop floor devices and permissions
summary: A scored readiness check that adapts the usual Copilot rollout gates to plants and hangars: manual revisions, export-controlled and customer data, shared devices, OT boundaries and a green-amber-red use-case tiering.
body:
# Copilot readiness check for a manufacturing plant: manuals, shop floor devices and permissions

## Purpose
A plant has problems an office does not: several revisions of the same manual, drawings under customer NDA, shared tablets, staff on shifts and machines that must never be touched by an AI. This check turns the usual rollout gates into a plant version you can score in a 60-minute workshop. Microsoft's own "Perform factory maintenance" scenario (Copilot and Copilot Studio) shows workers asking manuals, schematics and repair history in natural language, with a draft safety checklist and documentation of the result, and the page states it is a demonstration: check suitability against your own processes and regulations.

## Prerequisites
- A named sponsor, an IT owner, the quality manager, a safety officer and the works council or employee representation where applicable.
- Eligible licensing. Microsoft's licensing page lists Microsoft 365 F1 and F3 among eligible base plans for the Copilot add-on in commercial tenants; check current conditions and the service plan diagnostic for each user, because terms change.

## Scoring (0 = not in place, 1 = partly, 2 = in place)
| # | Gate | Evidence | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Manuals: current and superseded revisions are in separate libraries; status is metadata | Library list, sample of 20 documents | |
| 2 | Permissions: no Everyone or broad-group access on sites with drawings, customer data, HR or finance | Oversharing report, owner attestation | |
| 3 | Export-controlled and NDA data: sites identified, labelled, access limited to named people | Label report, export-control officer sign-off | |
| 4 | Sensitivity labels cover technical data and customer documents | Label coverage report | |
| 5 | Shared devices: sign-in method decided (Microsoft Entra shared device mode where it fits, QR or PIN sign-in, Intune app protection) | Device policy | |
| 6 | Use-case tiers approved (see below) and published | Signed tier list | |
| 7 | Prompt rules: no safety-critical or release decisions from Copilot output | Acceptable-use text | |
| 8 | OT boundary: Copilot has no write path to machines or control networks | Architecture note | |
| 9 | Champions per shift: at least one per 25 users (example ratio), on every shift | Champion list | |
| 10 | Feedback loop: a channel read daily during the pilot, incidents routed to security | Channel, runbook | |

Rule of thumb: a total of 17 or more and a score of 2 in each of gates 2, 3, 6, 7 and 8 allows a pilot. Fewer points: fix first. These thresholds are an example; set your own.

## Use-case tiers (example)
- Green (allowed from day one): meeting recaps, draft emails to suppliers (a human reads and sends), summaries of public or internal non-sensitive documents.
- Amber (allowed with review): rewrite of a work instruction in simpler language as a draft, A3 first draft from your notes, translation of internal notes, NCR text check for completeness. Output goes through the document owner.
- Red (not allowed): anything that replaces a manual, work card, certificate or sign-off; machine parameters; safety interlock decisions; release of aircraft or product. In aviation and MRO the certifying staff decide. Copilot output is never a release, never a substitute for the work card or the manual text.

## Worked example (invented data)
A plant with 600 staff scores: gate 1 = 1 (superseded files sit next to current ones in 6 of 20 sampled folders), gate 2 = 1 (two engineering sites use "Everyone except external users"), gate 3 = 2, gate 4 = 1, gate 5 = 1 (tablets use one shared account), gate 6 = 2, gate 7 = 2, gate 8 = 2, gate 9 = 1, gate 10 = 2. Total 15, and gate 2 is not yet 2. Decision: no pilot yet. Actions: split manuals into Effective and Archive (owner: quality manager, 3 weeks), fix the two sites (owner: IT, 1 week), set up per-person sign-in on tablets (owner: IT, 4 weeks). Re-score after 4 weeks; expected 18, pilot with 40 users on three shifts.

## Pitfalls
- Assuming Copilot "knows" which revision is valid. It uses what the user can access.
- Pilots only on the day shift. Night and weekend staff find the gaps.
- Treating shared devices as a detail. A shared account breaks audit trail and accountability.
- Letting someone connect an agent to machine data without review. Route that through the OT/IT data rules.

## Data protection
Prompts and results can contain personal data (names on a shift roster, observations about people). Agree rules with data protection and employee representation before the pilot. Do not paste customer-confidential or export-controlled content into tools that are not approved for it.

## Adapt to your environment
Replace tier examples with your own processes and update the gate list after the first incident review. Re-run gates 1 to 4 before each new wave, because content and permissions change.

title: Teams channel structure for a manufacturing plant with naming rules and channel type decisions
summary: A ready channel layout for a plant team (announcements, shift handover, maintenance, quality alerts, safety, supplier shared channel) with naming rules, limits from Microsoft Learn and decision rules for standard, private and shared channels.
body:
# Teams channel structure for a manufacturing plant with naming rules and channel type decisions

## Purpose
Teams in plants tend to fail in two ways: one team with 80 channels nobody reads, or one chat per machine that dies after a month. This entry gives a layout for one plant that you can adapt, with rules for naming, who gets which channel type, and what belongs in a channel, a chat, or a list.

## Facts that shape the design (Microsoft Learn, check current values)
- A team can have up to 25,000 members and 1,000 channels in total (standard, private and shared combined, including deleted channels). Treat these as ceilings, not goals.
- A shared channel lets you invite people who are not in the team, including people in other organisations via Microsoft Entra B2B direct connect (both organisations configure cross-tenant access settings). Guest accounts, including guests converted to members, cannot be added to a shared channel.
- A shared channel has its own SharePoint site that only channel owners and members can access, it inherits the parent team's sensitivity label, and it supports tabs except Stream, Planner and Forms. A shared channel cannot be moved to another team or converted to a standard channel. Cloning a team does not clone its shared channels.
- Shared channels are enabled by default; a channel policy controls creation and external sharing.

## Layout: one team per plant (example)
Team name: PLT-STG Plant Stuttgart (example). Owners: two named people (plant manager office and IT champion). Membership: static for office roles, dynamic (by plant and department attributes in Microsoft Entra) for operators, so people join and leave automatically.

| Channel | Type | Purpose | Tabs |
|---|---|---|---|
| General | standard | Announcements only, owners post | Plant news page |
| 01-Safety | standard | Observations, alerts, toolbox topics | Safety actions list |
| 02-Quality-Alerts | standard | Quality stops, containment messages | NCR list view |
| 03-Maintenance | standard | Breakdown requests and status | Maintenance list view |
| 04-Production-Planning | standard | Schedule changes, material shortages | Plan page |
| 05-Shift-Handover | standard | One post per shift per area | Handover list |
| 10-Area-Assembly | standard | Tier 2 for the area | KPI page, Actions view |
| 11-Area-Machining | standard | Tier 2 for the area | KPI page, Actions view |
| 90-Management | private | Personnel topics, cost topics | - |
| 95-Supplier-[name] | shared | Joint topic with one supplier | Joint list |

## Decision rules
1. Default to standard. Use private only when the content is restricted by law or policy (for example personnel matters), because a private channel has its own membership and its own SharePoint site; that fragments evidence.
2. Use a shared channel for external parties only when the other organisation has agreed cross-tenant settings and the content you share is limited to what the channel needs. Do not use it for audit evidence you must keep centrally.
3. One channel per area or process, never per machine. Machine history belongs in a list or the maintenance system.
4. A topic that needs a status belongs in a list; the channel carries only the notification.
5. Chat is for one-to-one coordination. Decisions get posted in a channel.

## Naming rules
Prefix with a two-digit number for sort order, then a short noun phrase, no abbreviations a new hire cannot guess. Keep names short because they truncate on phones. Avoid the restricted characters Teams lists and do not start with an underscore or period.

## Worked example (invented data)
A breakdown on a milling machine: the operator submits a breakdown form (a Lists form or a small Power Apps form linked from 03-Maintenance) that creates a list item (machine, symptom, stop time), and a flow posts the new item into the channel. The maintenance lead replies in the thread with "taken, ETA 20 min". At shift handover the open item appears automatically in the Shift-Handover view for the next team. After repair, the technician sets status Done and enters cause and parts in the list. The channel thread stays short; the list holds the history for MTBF and MTTR later.

## Lifecycle
Quarterly review: archive channels with no post for 90 days (example), check that every team has two owners, check membership of the private channel against the HR source. Define who may create teams and shared channels before rollout.

## Common mistakes
- Creating the channels first and the rules later.
- Planning a Planner tab in a shared channel (not supported).
- Putting 400 operators in a team with open posting in General. Limit posting to owners in General.
- Forgetting night shift when you define which channel is the "official" place for stops.

## Data protection
Channels hold names and time stamps of people. Align retention with data protection and, where it exists, employee representation before using channel posts for any performance topic.

title: SharePoint information architecture for a quality management system with hub, libraries and metadata
summary: A concrete SharePoint design for a QMS: hub and sites, libraries by status, content types, columns, permission groups, naming and migration steps, with the limits that matter for large document sets.
body:
# SharePoint information architecture for a quality management system with hub, libraries and metadata

## Purpose
A QMS has a few hundred controlled documents, thousands of records and a handful of registers (NCR, CAPA, audits, suppliers, calibration). If these are scattered across team folders, nobody can prove which revision is valid. This design gives you a structure that scales, keeps drafts out of reach and stays searchable.

## Facts that shape the design (Microsoft Learn)
- Hub sites are recommended over subsites. A subsite is a physical construct in the URL and policy features such as retention apply to the whole site collection; hub sites model relationships as links, so sites can move.
- Hub association does not change permissions. Rolled-up content is security trimmed. A site can belong to only one hub. Recommended maximum of 100 navigation links to sites in a hub.
- Lists and libraries: up to 30 million items per library. The list view threshold of 5,000 items cannot be changed in SharePoint Online; use indexed columns, filtered views and folders sparingly to keep views working.

## Site design
| Site | Template | Purpose | Owner group |
|---|---|---|---|
| QMS Hub | Communication site, hub | Navigation, news, policy, manual | QMS owner |
| QMS Documents | Team or communication site | Controlled documents (effective, draft, archive) | Document control |
| QMS Records | Team site | Quality records by process and year | Quality |
| QMS Registers | Team site | NCR, CAPA, audit plan, supplier, calibration lists | Quality |
| Supplier Quality | Team site | Supplier files and certificates | Purchasing quality |
Use separate sites when owners, permissions or retention differ. Do not nest.

## Libraries in "QMS Documents"
1. Effective: only released documents. Readers: all staff (or the audience of the document).
2. Drafts: authors and reviewers only.
3. Archive: superseded and obsolete documents, read-only for most, access for auditors.
Moving a document between libraries is a flow, not manual copying. Keep one number across libraries so history is traceable.

## Content types and columns
Content types: Procedure, Work instruction, Form template, Specification, Policy.
Site columns (reuse across libraries): Document number (text, indexed), Revision (text), Status (choice: Draft, In review, Effective, Superseded, Obsolete; indexed), Process area (managed metadata term set), Applies to site (choice, multi-value), Process owner (person), Effective date (date), Next review (date), Training needed (yes/no), Customer-specific (yes/no).
Use managed metadata for Process area so the term set is maintained once. Keep choice columns short.

## Permissions
Groups: QMS Admins (full control, two people), Process Owners (edit in Drafts, read in Effective; the release flow runs under a service identity that is allowed to move documents), Readers (read in Effective), Auditors (read in all, time-boxed). Break inheritance on the library level only, never on single files. Check regularly with an access review. Customer-specific documents may need a separate library with a sensitivity label.

## Versioning and approval
Turn on content approval and major and minor versions in Drafts. Keep minor versions invisible to readers. Documentation on versioning is partly written for SharePoint Server, so test the behaviour in your tenant. Automatic version limits are fine for drafts; for records use retention labels (see the audit evidence entry).

## Naming and numbering
Document number pattern example: [process area]-[type]-[running number], for example QA-PR-0042 (example only). Title shows what, not who. Never put the revision in the file name; use the Revision column.

## Worked example (invented data)
Migration of 640 documents: 410 are current, 170 superseded, 60 duplicates. Steps: export the inventory to Excel, assign number and status, delete duplicates after owner confirmation, upload the 410 to Drafts with metadata, approve in batches of 50, move to Effective by the release flow; upload 170 superseded to Archive. Result: Effective library 410 items, index on Document number and Status, default view filtered to Status Effective, sort by Process area. Search for "torque" returns only effective documents for regular users.

## RACI
| Task | QMS owner | Doc control | Process owner | IT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Metadata model | A | R | C | C |
| Release a document | I | R | A | - |
| Site and permissions | A | C | I | R |
| Yearly structure review | A | R | C | C |

## Common mistakes
- Folders for status or year. Use metadata and views.
- Subsites for departments. Use hub association.
- No owner for the term set.
- Releasing without a number system. Two documents with the same number cost an audit finding.
- Giving everybody edit rights "to be quick".

## Adapt to your environment
Align status words and numbering with your quality manual and your certification body, add site-specific audiences, and decide whether customer-controlled documents sit in the same library. Confirm limits in current Microsoft documentation before the migration.

title: Frontline rollout plan for plant and hangar staff: 12 weeks, shared devices and RACI
summary: A 12-week rollout plan for Teams, Shifts, tasks and approvals on the shop floor: pilot gates, shared-device sign-in options, training slots on every shift, RACI and a worked pilot example.
body:
# Frontline rollout plan for plant and hangar staff: 12 weeks, shared devices and RACI

## Purpose
Office rollouts assume everyone has a laptop and a desk. On the shop floor people share devices, wear gloves, work three shifts and have ten minutes at shift start. This plan gets a first useful scenario live in 12 weeks and scales only after the pilot proves it.

## What Microsoft documents (check current pages)
- Frontline licenses: Microsoft 365 F1 and F3; enterprise licenses can also be used. F3 includes features F1 does not, such as Power Apps and Power Automate.
- Frontline solutions: Teams chat and notifications, Walkie Talkie, Shifts, Lists, Planner, Approvals, Viva Connections, Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI.
- Frontline teams can use dynamic membership, static membership or a mix. Microsoft recommends a pilot and offers a Frontline Solutions Success Kit.
- Planner can publish task lists to specific teams (for example daily start-up checks) and managers can monitor completion; this needs a team targeting hierarchy.
- Shared devices: Microsoft Entra shared device mode (Android, iOS, iPadOS) gives single sign-in and single sign-out; QR code and PIN sign-in is supported on iOS, iPadOS and Android; domain-less sign-in is available in Teams on iOS and Android; Intune app protection policies can block copy, save and transfer to apps that do not support shared device mode. Multifactor authentication adds friction on shared devices, so test it; if it is not feasible, rely on Conditional Access with device compliance, trusted locations or managed devices.

## Pick one first scenario
Choose the scenario with a clear owner and a visible gain, for example: shift schedule and swaps (Shifts), daily equipment start-up checklist (Planner or Lists), breakdown call (Teams channel plus list), or approvals for scrap or overtime (Approvals). Do not launch all four.

## 12-week timeline
| Weeks | Activity | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| 1-2 | Scope, sponsor, owners, works council briefing, device inventory, licence check | Scope signed |
| 3-4 | Teams structure, dynamic groups, Shifts setup, policies, shared-device sign-in design | Test group works on two device types |
| 5 | Pilot prep: champions per shift, 20-minute training at shift start, QR posters | Champions trained |
| 6-8 | Pilot with one line on all three shifts (about 40 people) | Weekly review |
| 9 | Pilot review against metrics, fix list | Go or no-go for wave 2 |
| 10-12 | Wave 2: next two lines, support hours at shift change | Adoption and incident metrics |

## Metrics (decide before the pilot)
- Active use per week: share of pilot users who opened the scenario at least 3 times.
- Time to find a swap partner or to log a breakdown (baseline versus pilot).
- Open service-desk tickets per 100 users.
- Qualitative: 5 questions to team leaders at week 8.
Never publish individual usage rankings; report per team. A standard Planner task list published "for each team" counts one completion per team; per-person counts need the "for each team member" list type and an agreement with the works council on who sees them.

## RACI
| Activity | Sponsor | Plant manager | IT/Endpoint | Champions | HR/Works council |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scope and success measures | A | R | C | C | C |
| Device and sign-in design | I | C | A/R | C | I |
| Training slots on each shift | I | A | C | R | C |
| Support and escalation | I | A | R | R | I |
| Data protection review | I | C | C | I | A/R |

## Worked example (invented data)
Pilot line: 42 operators in 3 shifts, 6 shared Android tablets. Sign-in: QR code and PIN, Intune app protection on, single sign-out at shift end. Scenario: daily start-up check as a published Planner task list plus Shifts for swaps. Week 6 result: 31 of 42 completed the check at least 3 times (74 percent). Four tablets were charging at the wrong place, 9 tickets were about PIN resets. Fix: charging docks next to the board, PIN reset instructions on the back of the poster. Week 9 decision: go for wave 2, because use is 85 percent in week 8 and tickets fell to 3.

## Hangar and plant specifics
- Clean-area, ESD and foreign object rules decide whether phones or tablets may be used at the aircraft or machine. Align with the safety and quality managers; use fixed screens or lanyards where they require it.
- Gloves and noise: use large buttons, QR codes, Walkie Talkie for voice. Test with real gloves.
- Shift workers need training in paid time and in their own shift, with a champion who works that shift.

## Common mistakes
- Training only the day shift.
- Starting without the works council. Shifts and task monitoring touch working time and people data.
- Individual accounts forced on a shared tablet without a sign-out plan; or one shared account for everyone.
- Counting licenses assigned as adoption.

## Adapt to your environment
Adjust the timeline to your shutdown calendar, replace the scenario, and check licensing, device support and Teams policies in your tenant. The numbers here are examples, set your own gates.

title: Shopfloor KPI board design: SQDC tiles, definitions, refresh cadence and escalation rules
summary: A design spec for a digital SQDC board: tile definition card, example tiles with formulas and a worked calculation, visual rules, Power BI and Teams setup, refresh and escalation rules.
body:
# Shopfloor KPI board design: SQDC tiles, definitions, refresh cadence and escalation rules

## Purpose
A KPI board only works if everyone reads the same number the same way and knows what happens when it is red. This spec defines the tile, the rules for design and refresh, and the escalation logic. It fits a physical board with a digital twin of the numbers, or a screen at the line.

## Prerequisites
- Data sources decided per KPI (MES, ERP, quality system, Forms or Lists).
- Power BI workspace with an owner and a semantic model, or Power BI reports based on a shared dataset. Check licensing for who may view (viewers may need a license depending on capacity and workspace type; check in your tenant).
- Agreed definitions (see the OEE definition sheet for the OEE tile).

## The tile definition card
Fill one card per tile before building.
Name; Category (S, Q, D, C); Purpose in one sentence; Formula in words; Unit; Source and table; Time grain (shift, day); Target and who set it; Colour rule; Refresh time; Owner (person); Escalation rule; Last change of definition (date).

## Example tiles
| Tile | Formula | Source | Colour rule (example) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Safety: reported near misses per week | Count of near-miss reports in the week | Forms or list | Green if at least target; low counts are suspicious, not good |
| Safety: open safety actions overdue | Count of safety actions past due date | Actions list | Red if 1 or more |
| Quality: first pass yield | Units passed first time without rework or scrap divided by units entering the step | MES/quality | Red if below target for the shift |
| Quality: scrap rate | Scrapped units divided by produced units | MES | Amber within 0.5 point of limit |
| Delivery: on-time delivery (OTD) | Order lines shipped on or before the promised date divided by lines due | ERP | Red below target |
| Delivery: schedule adherence | Units produced against units planned for the shift | MES | Green at plan or above, amber 90 to under 100 percent, red below 90 percent (example) |
| Cost: OEE or labour efficiency | per definition sheet | MES/Eventhouse | Per target |
| Cost: overtime hours vs plan | Overtime hours divided by plan | HR/time system | Red above plan |

## Design rules
1. At most six tiles per screen; Safety first and largest.
2. Each tile shows: today, a 14-day trend line, the target line, and a time stamp "data as of".
3. Do not use colour alone: add an arrow or text (OK, WATCH, STOP) for people with colour vision deficiency.
4. Same layout for every line so people can read any board.
5. Numbers are shown for the team or line, not for a person.
6. Drill-down goes to the top three causes (Pareto), not to a data dump.

## Build in Microsoft 365
- Power BI report with one page per area; a mobile layout for the team leader.
- Embed the report as a tab in the area Teams channel; use Power BI data alerts to post a message in the channel when a tile turns red (data alerts are set on dashboard tiles such as cards, KPIs and gauges; check the options available in your tenant and for your data source).
- A Lists-based Actions register next to the board. Any red tile gets an action there.
- Refresh: set the semantic model schedule to complete before the shift start, for example 05:45 for a 06:00 start. For live lines use a DirectQuery or streaming approach only if the source can handle it; start with scheduled refresh.
- Row-level security if lines should not see other lines.

## Escalation rule (example)
- A tile red for one shift: the team leader acts and notes the cause in the register.
- Red for two consecutive shifts or three of the last seven: it appears on the Tier 2 agenda.
- Safety red: stops the meeting and goes to the area manager immediately.
- Someone resolves the item before the next shift or states a decision date.

## Worked example (invented data)
Line 2, yesterday: 1,200 units entered final test, 1,152 passed first time, 36 reworked, 12 scrapped. FPY = 1,152 / 1,200 = 96.0 percent. Target 97.5 percent, so Quality is red. Scrap rate = 12 / 1,200 = 1.0 percent. OTD for the week: 188 order lines due, 171 shipped on time. OTD = 171 / 188 = 90.96 percent, shown as 91.0 percent, target 95 percent: red. The previous shift was also below target, so this is the second red shift for FPY and so the item goes to the Tier 2 agenda and the Pareto shows 21 of 48 defects came from one fixture.

## Common mistakes
- Target without owner.
- Definitions that change silently. Put a change log on the card and note it on the board.
- Rolling up percentages incorrectly: average of daily percentages is not the weekly percentage; recompute from counts.
- Gaming risk when people are judged on a single number. Pair yield with rework and scrap.
- No owner for data quality; a blank tile is worse than an old one, so show the time stamp.

## Data protection
Do not display names with individual output. If you collect observations about people, involve data protection and the employee representation first.

title: OT/IT data rules for manufacturers: zones, allowed flows and ownership with Azure IoT Operations
summary: A rulebook for connecting plant data to Microsoft cloud: data classes, zone model, allowed flows, tag ownership, naming, change control and a worked example from an OPC UA tag to Fabric, with write-back forbidden by default.
body:
# OT/IT data rules for manufacturers: zones, allowed flows and ownership with Azure IoT Operations

## Purpose
When plant data moves to the cloud, two cultures meet: OT (availability, safety, change windows) and IT (security, scale, speed). Without written rules, you get shadow gateways, shared credentials and tags nobody owns. This is a rulebook you can adapt and sign by both sides before the first data flow goes live.

## What Microsoft documents (check current version)
Azure IoT Operations runs on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters at the edge. It includes an MQTT broker, connectors (including one for OPC UA and one for HTTP/REST), data flows to transform and route data, an operations experience for OT users, the Azure Device Registry with a schema registry, and Akri services for discovery. Documented destinations include Event Grid and other MQTT brokers, Event Hubs or Kafka, Azure Data Lake Storage, Microsoft Fabric OneLake and Azure Data Explorer. The documentation states it can operate offline for a period (up to 72 hours at the time of reading, with possible degradation). A newer Essentials SKU is described as supporting single-node clusters only and not supporting the OPC UA connector, so check the SKU against your needs before design. Microsoft Defender for IoT is the product for OT network monitoring.

## Zones (reference model)
Use the ISA-95 or Purdue style levels as the vocabulary your OT team already knows: Level 0-1 sensors, drives and PLCs; Level 2 supervisory control and HMI; Level 3 site operations (MES, historian); Level 4-5 enterprise and cloud. The edge cluster sits at a defined boundary, normally in a DMZ between site operations and enterprise. Decide the exact placement with your OT security lead; do not assume.

## Data classes
| Class | Examples | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| A Telemetry | Temperatures, states, counters | May leave the site after review of each tag group |
| B Quality and trace | Test results, serials, batch numbers | May leave under the quality retention rule; customer terms apply |
| C Process IP | Recipes, setpoints, programs | Stays at the site unless the process owner and legal sign off |
| D Personal | Operator IDs, badge data | Only with data protection approval; pseudonymise at the edge where possible |

## The rules
1. Read-only by default. No write path from IT or cloud (including any AI agent) to controllers. A write path needs a separate change request, safety review and a named approver on the OT side.
2. Every tag has an owner, a unit, a data class and a sampling rate in a register before it is published.
3. Names follow one pattern: enterprise/site/area/line/cell/signal (example: acme/stg/machining/l2/cnc4/spindle_temp_c, invented). Units in the name or schema, UTC time stamps.
4. Connections are made by service identities with the minimum role, never with personal or shared admin accounts. Secrets live in a vault, never in code, tickets or chat.
5. No direct cloud-to-PLC connection. Data goes through the edge broker and data flow.
6. Change control: adding, removing or re-scaling a tag is a change; OT approves, IT builds, both log it. Plan maintenance in agreed windows.
7. Time: devices use a common time source; document the drift tolerance.
8. Availability: define what happens during an outage; the edge buffers, the cloud tolerates gaps, and dashboards show "data as of".
9. Retention and deletion: raw telemetry kept for the agreed period (set it with quality and legal), aggregates longer. Check customer contracts.
10. Incident: OT and security share a contact list; an unexplained data flow is stopped first, explained after.

## Worked example (invented data)
Goal: spindle temperature alarm for CNC 4. The OT engineer registers the tag (owner: maintenance engineer; unit degrees Celsius; class A; sampling 1 Hz). The OPC UA connector publishes to the broker topic acme/stg/machining/l2/cnc4/spindle_temp_c. A data flow filters to one value every 10 seconds and sends it to Fabric (Eventhouse) for the rule "above limit for 3 minutes". Result: the maintenance planner gets a notification, an action is created in the Lists register, no write-back exists. Review at 30 days: 3 alerts, 2 true. Tag stays; sampling stays at 10 seconds.

## RACI
| Activity | OT engineering | IT/cloud | Security | Process owner | Data protection |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tag register entry | R | C | I | A | I |
| Build data flow | C | R | C | I | I |
| Class D approval | I | C | C | C | A |
| Write-back request | A/R | C | C | C | I |
| Incident handling | R | R | A | I | C |

## Common mistakes
- Treating the edge cluster like a normal IT server (patching during production).
- Publishing all tags "because we can".
- No owner for the tag after the engineer leaves.
- Connecting an AI assistant directly to live machine commands. Use it for analysis and recommendations; people operate the machines.

## Adapt to your environment
Align zone placement with your OT security standard (for example IEC 62443 based) and your own network segmentation; check the Learn pages for the version and SKU you deploy.

title: OEE definition sheet: one agreed calculation, loss categories and edge cases for multi-line plants
summary: A one-page definition of OEE that the whole plant signs: time model, formulas, loss codes, ruling on changeovers, micro-stops, rework and planned stops, a fully calculated example and a change log.
body:
# OEE definition sheet: one agreed calculation, loss categories and edge cases for multi-line plants

## Purpose
Two lines, two spreadsheets, two OEE numbers that cannot be compared. This sheet fixes the calculation and the rulings on edge cases once, so reports, dashboards and the Power BI measures all agree. Put it in a controlled library with a version number and an owner.

## Basic formulas
OEE = Availability x Performance x Quality
- Availability = run time / planned production time
- Performance = (ideal cycle time x total count) / run time
- Quality = good count / total count
Equivalent shortcut: OEE = (good count x ideal cycle time) / planned production time. Use it as a cross-check.

## Time model (decide once)
1. Calendar time: all time in the period.
2. Less time with no planned production (no order, no shift, plant closure): the result is planned production time.
3. Less stops (breakdowns, changeovers, material shortage, waiting): the result is run time.
4. Less slow cycles and micro-stops: the result is fully productive time for the output made.
5. Less rejected units: the result is fully productive time for good output.
Decision for your plant: is no-order time excluded (OEE) or included (TEEP)? Write down the choice. This sheet assumes it is excluded.

## Rulings on edge cases (starting position; change where your plant differs and record the reason)
| Case | Ruling | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Planned breaks and meetings | Excluded from planned production time | Not available for production |
| Changeover and setup | Counted as availability loss | SMED improves it; hiding it hides the opportunity |
| Planned maintenance | Excluded only if scheduled in the plan before the week starts; otherwise a loss | Prevents moving breakdowns into "planned" |
| Micro-stop | Stop shorter than [threshold, set by line, example 2 minutes] counts as performance loss; longer is availability loss | Needs one threshold per machine class |
| Reduced speed | Performance loss | Compare with ideal cycle time, not the standard |
| Rework | Not good count unless made good first time (quality loss); reworked units do not enter good count again | First pass logic |
| Start-up scrap | Quality loss | Visible and improvable |
| Co-products and packs | Count in the unit of the ideal cycle time; document conversion factors | Avoid double counting |
| Waiting for material | Availability loss, coded as a loss reason | Process owner is not the machine |
| No operator | Availability loss with a separate code | Staffing decision visible |

## Ideal cycle time
Source: the fastest repeatable cycle proven on the machine (or the machine's rated speed), approved by engineering, kept per product family in a table with owner and date. Never use the average actual cycle as ideal.

## Loss codes (six big losses as a structure)
Breakdowns; setup and adjustments; minor stops and idling; reduced speed; start-up rejects; production rejects. Add your own sub-codes, but keep the six groups so plants can be compared.

## Worked example (invented data)
One shift: 480 minutes. Planned breaks: 30 minutes. Planned production time = 450 minutes. Downtime: changeover 30 minutes, breakdown 24 minutes: total 54 minutes. Run time = 450 - 54 = 396 minutes. Ideal cycle time = 0.5 minute per part. Total count = 640. Good count = 608.
- Availability = 396 / 450 = 0.880
- Performance = (0.5 x 640) / 396 = 320 / 396 = 0.808
- Quality = 608 / 640 = 0.950
- OEE = 0.880 x 0.808 x 0.950 = 0.675 with the rounded factors (0.6756 unrounded), or 67.6 percent.
Cross-check: (608 x 0.5) / 450 = 304 / 450 = 0.6756. Losses in minutes of the 450 planned: reduced speed and micro-stops 76 (16.9 percent), stops 54 (12.0 percent, of which changeover 30), rejects 16 (3.6 percent), fully productive 304 (67.6 percent). The biggest single loss is performance: analyse micro-stops and speed before the changeover.

## Data and tooling
- Capture states with time stamps from the machine (state events) or from operator entries with a mandatory loss reason. Mixed sources need the same codes.
- Build the measures once in a shared Power BI semantic model so every report reuses them; do not recalculate OEE in each report.
- Aggregate over time from counts and minutes, never by averaging daily percentages. Weekly OEE is the sum of (good count x ideal cycle time) over all products divided by total planned production time.

## Governance
Owner: continuous improvement manager. Approver: plant manager. Review: yearly or when a new line type arrives. Keep a change log (date, change, reason, effect on reported OEE) so a jump in the numbers can be explained. When the definition changes, restate the last 12 months or mark the break in the trend.

## Common mistakes
- Comparing OEE across plants with different rulings.
- Using OEE as a personal performance metric; it measures the process.
- Targets copied from a generic benchmark such as the often quoted 85 percent. Use your own baseline and the loss data.
- Excluding changeovers because "they are necessary".
- OEE above 100 percent: wrong ideal cycle time or counting error.

title: Part-145 digital records checklist for MRO: handover, task cards and Microsoft 365 controls
summary: A checklist for MRO organisations using Microsoft 365 around their maintenance system: system-of-record decision, shift handover content, integrity, retention, access, offline fallback and AI limits, with a worked handover example.
body:
# Part-145 digital records checklist for MRO: handover, task cards and Microsoft 365 controls

## Purpose
Many MRO organisations run their maintenance system for task cards and release, and use Microsoft 365 for everything around it: handover, planning notes, meetings, supplier chats, training. The risk is a record that matters ending up in a place that nobody controls. This checklist helps the quality manager decide what goes where, and what must be true before it does.

## Important limits
- This is a planning aid, not regulatory advice. Check every item against the current regulation, your Maintenance Organisation Exposition (MOE), your approved procedures and your competent authority.
- Certifying staff decide on release. Copilot output is never a release, never a substitute for the work card, the maintenance data or the manual text.
- The regulatory references below come from a manufacturer's technical article, not an official source; confirm them. The article states that Part-145 point 145.A.47(c) requires relevant information to be passed on at shift and task changes, with the procedure described in the MOE, and that the management-system records point (145.A.200) is not a handover requirement. Treat the numbers as leads to verify.

## 1. System of record (decide first)
| Item | System of record | Microsoft 365 role | Approved by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Task cards, work orders, release | Maintenance system | Link only | Quality manager |
| Defect cards | Maintenance system | Notification | Quality manager |
| Shift handover | Decide: maintenance system or controlled list | If SharePoint: controlled list, see below | MOE procedure |
| Procedures and MOE | Document control | Controlled library | Quality manager |
| Training and authorisations | HR or training system | Read-only report | Training manager |
| Tool calibration | Tool system | Reminders | Stores manager |
| Meeting notes, planning chat | Microsoft 365 | Normal, not a record of work | - |
Rule: one place per record. If Microsoft 365 holds a record, the procedure says so.

## 2. Shift handover content (check against your MOE)
Per aircraft registration and work order: tasks completed, tasks open and state, new defects raised, defects closed, parts and material outstanding, tooling or special equipment in use, general issues (safety, access, ground support, shortages). "Nothing to report" must be a recorded answer, not an empty field. A purely verbal handover is a known human-factors weakness; the written record is the base and the talk adds to it.

## 3. Handover list design (if you use SharePoint)
List "Shift handover", one item per aircraft per shift: Date, Shift (early, late, night), Aircraft registration (choice), Work order, From (person), To (person), Completed tasks, Open tasks, New defects, Closed defects, Parts outstanding, Issues, Nothing to report (yes/no), Acknowledged by (person), Acknowledged on.
Rules: required columns; acknowledgement by the receiving person; no deletion by users (use a custom permission level without Delete Items and check it in your tenant; delete only for admins); versioning on; view "Open by aircraft" for the oncoming shift.

## 4. Integrity checklist
- [ ] Documents that are controlled (procedures, instructions) are in a library with approval and version history.
- [ ] Items that must not be changed after sign-off carry a record retention label; understand that a locked record blocks editing and deletion (an unlocked record can be edited but not deleted), and that a regulatory record cannot be unlabeled by anyone. Choose with the quality manager and legal.
- [ ] Version limits do not remove versions you need to keep. Retention policy and holds override limits; records block version deletion.
- [ ] Audit log is on and searchable; the quality manager knows how to request an extract.
- [ ] Backup and restore tested: the recycle bin is not a backup.

## 5. Access and identity
- [ ] Named accounts only; no shared accounts for handover entries.
- [ ] Certifying staff stamps or numbers are not typed into free-text fields unless the procedure allows it.
- [ ] Access reviewed twice a year; leavers removed at once.
- [ ] Guests and suppliers do not see aircraft records. If supplier collaboration is needed, use a separate shared channel or site with only the topic data.
- [ ] Conditional Access applies to the sites; the hangar tablets have a documented sign-in method.

## 6. Retention and deletion
Retention periods come from the regulation, your MOE and your customers' contracts, not from this checklist. Record the source for each class (for example "work record class: period per MOE section X"; fill in your own). Do not enable auto-deletion until the quality manager has signed the table.

## 7. Availability and fallback
- [ ] What happens when Microsoft 365 or the network is down? A paper or offline handover form exists and is entered afterwards with a time stamp.
- [ ] The maximum tolerable outage is written down and accepted.

## 8. AI use rules
- [ ] Copilot may summarise meeting notes and draft emails; people verify and send.
- [ ] No handover entry is created from AI output without the person reading and owning it.
- [ ] No AI text replaces a work card step, a limit value or a manual quote; always read the source.

## Worked example (invented data, fictional registration)
Late shift to night shift, aircraft EXAMPLE-AC1, work order WO-4711 (invented): Completed: left main gear inspection tasks 1-6. Open: task 7 waiting for parts, state 50 percent. New defects: cabin reading light inoperable, defect card raised. Closed defects: none. Parts outstanding: one consumable on order, expected before the night shift. Issues: ground power unit unavailable until 23:00. The oncoming lead opens the list view "Open by aircraft", reads the entry, acknowledges it and phones the outgoing lead for the parts question. The audit trail shows who wrote the entry and who acknowledged it, and when.

## Common mistakes
- Treating the handover as chat. Chat is searchable but not controlled.
- Duplicating records in the maintenance system and SharePoint that drift apart.
- Letting auto-delete run on an unchecked class.
- Forgetting the staff data aspect: handover entries show names and shifts; agree usage with data protection and employee representation.

## Adapt to your environment
Map each point to the exact MOE section and procedure number in your organisation, assign an owner and a check date per item, and review after every audit finding.
